title: Rami Library among Türkiye’s first stewards in Heritage Adapts!
raw_text: Rami Library Rami Library in İstanbul has joined Heritage Adapts!, a global campaign helping heritage sites prepare for climate change. Announced today at COP31, it is one of five participants from host country Türkiye, and more than 100 across 59 countries. IFLA is a leadership partner in the campaign. Rami Library is already a model for sustainable libraries: this year it won first place in the Large-Scale Project category of the 2026 IFLA Green Library Award , for transforming a 19th-century military barracks into a climate-resilient public space. Libraries’ buildings, collections and archives face growing climate risks. For Rami Library, that means an increased risk of flooding, for example. Türkiye’s Directorate General of Libraries and Publications has also confirmed its support for the campaign: “ We consider this cooperation an opportunity to share our experience in heritage conservation and sustainable library development, while benefiting from international expertise, practical tools and the collective knowledge of participating institutions .” — Taner Beyoğlu, Director-General of Libraries and Publications, Ministry of Culture and Tourism of the Republic of Türkiye Rami Library joins a diverse group of heritage stewards in Türkiye, from a workshop reviving traditional İznik tile-making to the ancient city of Olympos and the Silk Road town of Mudurnu. title: AI is Reshaping the Role of Academic Librarians; Elsevier Releases Librarian of the Future Report
raw_text: From an Elsevier News Release: Today, Elsevier shares findings from its global Librarian of the Future research, revealing how artificial intelligence (AI) and changing research needs are reshaping the role of academic librarians. Drawing on insights from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders, the report reveals a profession harnessing AI while also anticipating a greater role in helping institutions navigate its risks. The findings point to an opportunity for librarians to become more closely involved in institutional decision-making and strengthen their position as strategic partners in research. [Clip] Librarians expect their role in AI to grow meaningfully. Almost all (95%) expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years, while 82% believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers and 76% believe they should play a role in AI governance. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) While librarians are ready to contribute to AI initiatives, only 30% report their institution has implemented an AI policy. These findings highlight a potential gap between the pace of AI adoption and institutional preparedness. With this in mind, the report points to an increasingly important role for librarians in helping researchers navigate trusted information, responsible AI use and research integrity. Source: Librarian of the Future Report (2026) Jim O’Donnell, University Librarian

title: llm 0.37.3
raw_text: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
raw_text: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. title: Report: “New Kickstarter Campaign Rethinks E-Book Ownership and Digital Lending”
raw_text: From TechCrunch: Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.” That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project , an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra . If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries. To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.” [Clip] The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries. title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
raw_text: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. title: Nieuwe ideeën voor lokale journalistiek en de bibliotheek tijdens Dutch Design Week
raw_text: Hoe kunnen bibliotheken en lokale mediapartners samen bijdragen aan een sterke lokale democratie? Tijdens een ontwerpsessie op de Dutch Design Week werkten bibliotheekprofessionals, journalisten en andere maatschappelijke partners aan concrete programmaconcepten die vanaf 2027 mogelijk als pilot van start gaan. De sessie is een vervolg op de whitepaper Journalistiek, de bibliotheek en burgerschap die verkent welke kansen samenwerking tussen bibliotheken en journalistiek biedt. Onder begeleiding van Daniëlle Arets, lector Designing Journalism aan de Fontys School voor Journalistiek, gingen deelnemers aan de slag met het ontwikkelen van programmaconcepten. De sessie leverde niet alleen inspirerende ideeën op, maar ook nieuwe verbindingen tussen organisaties die elkaar hebben gevonden in hun gezamenlijke maatschappelijke opdracht. Jongerenredactie als plek voor onderzoek en ontmoeting Tijdens de ontwerpsessie ontstonden verschillende veelbelovende concepten, die allemaal inzetten op ontmoeting, betrokkenheid en het versterken van de verbinding tussen inwoners, bibliotheek en mediapartners. Zo werd gewerkt aan een jongerenredactie waarin jongeren, onder begeleiding van een lokale omroep, onderzoek doen naar onderwerpen die spelen in hun eigen omgeving. De jongeren leren zo journalistieke vaardigheden en dragen actief bij aan het publieke gesprek. title: Mem Is Shutting Down
Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse
raw_text: A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza. Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC . The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak , supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago. This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons. title: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365
raw_text: A hidden defect in Microsoft's cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the company's history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft's report lists the incident's final status as "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents." Microsoft's preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14. The outage started on November 12 and quickly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft's cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft's incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the company's status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report , and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft's service-health updates .
